screens.title: Network Telemetry and Streaming Data
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll move from the familiar world of periodic polling to a push-based telemetry model that streams device data in near real time. You will learn why SNMP polling—where a management station asks devices for snapshots every few minutes—can miss transient events, and how streaming telemetry captures high-granularity operational state to enable faster troubleshooting and proactive detection. We will explore the main protocols that make streaming possible, including gNMI and NETCONF subscriptions, and the data formats those protocols commonly use: efficient binary encoding with Google Protocol Buffers and human-readable formats like JSON or XML. You’ll also see a practical, end-to-end architecture: devices push to a collector, messages can be buffered with a broker when needed, data lands in a time-series store, and dashboards visualize trends. By the end you’ll understand where streaming telemetry fits in an enterprise design and a simple scenario—collecting interface octets at sub-second intervals—to illustrate why this model matters operationally. Think about a recent transient outage: could higher-frequency telemetry have revealed a microburst earlier?

screens.title: SNMP Polling vs Streaming Telemetry
screens.narratorSegment: Begin with a clear definition: SNMP polling is a pull-based model where a management station requests specific MIB objects periodically, producing discrete snapshots of device state. In contrast, streaming telemetry is a push-based model where devices continuously send operational data to a collector, often at sub-second rates. A concrete example helps: if you poll interface counters every five minutes, a brief microburst that causes packet loss for twenty seconds can be invisible in the five-minute snapshot. Streaming telemetry configured to sample every second will capture that microburst as a series of high-resolution points you can analyze. A common misconception is that polling is always lighter on the network; in large-scale deployments polling thousands of devices frequently creates larger aggregate overhead and C P U load than efficiently encoded, device-driven streams. To test this, compare aggregate bytes on the management plane during a polling schedule versus the same metrics streamed at one-second intervals encoded with Protocol Buffers. Takeaway: streaming gives fidelity and timeliness; however, you must design retention and volume controls so you don't overwhelm storage or processors. SNMP Polling vs Streaming Telemetry means polling gives periodic snapshots that can miss short events; streaming telemetry provides continuous, high-resolution data for accurate, proactive operations.. In practical terms, why polling snapshots miss transient events and how streaming fixes that. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › SNMP vs Streaming
Comparison

Polling snapshots

Periodic SNMP polls return MIB values on demand. Simple, but limited in timeliness and granularity.
  • Scalability: Polling thousands of devices often increases traffic and CPU load.
  • Granularity: Polling interval determines visibility; sub-minute events can be missed.
  • Timeliness: Data can be stale by the time it is collected and processed.
Concrete example
A five-minute poll misses a 20-second microburst that a one-second telemetry stream would capture as multiple high-resolution samples.
Core Concept

Streaming telemetry

Devices push selected YANG-path-based data continuously to a collector. This is efficient and near real time when encoded with GPB or JSON.
Higher fidelity
Sub-second samples
Scalable pushes
Publishers control cadence
Proactive monitoring
Anomaly detection
Design caution
Manage volume
Key Takeaway

Streaming telemetry provides timelier, higher-resolution data than SNMP polling, but it requires planning for data volume and retention.

screens.title: What is Streaming Telemetry?
screens.narratorSegment: Streaming telemetry is a push-based network monitoring model where devices send operational data to a collector without waiting for a poll. Define the model clearly: devices publish telemetry for configured YANG paths, and subscriptions control what is sent and at what cadence. Benefits are concrete: near real-time visibility lets you detect performance bottlenecks as they happen, higher granularity captures short-lived events, and scalability improves because devices decide what to send and when. A practical example: configure a sensor that streams interface in-octets every second for a critical uplink. The collector aggregates these samples and detects spikes that match a service degradation window. A common misconception is that streaming always increases network load; in practice, efficient encodings like Protocol Buffers reduce payload size and allow you to select only necessary YANG paths, minimizing overhead. Closing thought: streaming telemetry is a design pattern—use it where fidelity, timeliness, and proactive analytics matter most. Streaming Telemetry — definition & benefits

Devices continuously publish configured YANG-path data to a collector at chosen intervals and encodings.
Real-time visibility
Higher granularity
Scalable publishes

screens.title: gNMI and NETCONF Subscriptions
screens.narratorSegment: gNMI and NETCONF subscriptions are the primary protocols for streaming telemetry covered in this chapter. Define gNMI as a gRPC-based interface that uses YANG to define data and typically encodes payloads with Google Protocol Buffers for efficient binary serialization. gNMI supports one-time retrievals and continuous subscriptions; subscription modes include sample and on-change, allowing you to tailor cadence and triggers. NETCONF subscriptions extend NETCONF to push updates, often using XML or JSON encodings and the same YANG models. A concrete example: a gNMI subscription might sample an interface statistics path every second with JSON IETF or PROTO encoding. A common misconception is that gNMI always uses GPB—some implementations allow JSON IETF encoding for readability. Why it matters: protocol and encoding choices affect payload size, parsing load, and interoperability with collectors and analytics engines. Takeaway: choose gNMI for high-performance streaming, and use NETCONF subscriptions when integrating into existing NETCONF-based management stacks. gNMI and NETCONF Subscriptions means gnmi is grpc-based and efficient with gpb; netconf subscriptions extend xml/json-based netconf to support pushes. both rely on yang for data modeling.. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › gNMI & NETCONF
Definition

gNMI and NETCONF Subscriptions

Both protocols rely on YANG models to identify the data to stream, but they differ in transport and typical encodings.
gNMI
gRPC transport, supports PROTO/JSON encodings, efficient for high-frequency streams.
Modes: one-time, sample, on-change
NETCONF Subscriptions
Extension to NETCONF allowing pushes, commonly uses XML or JSON encodings, leverages existing NETCONF infrastructure.
Concrete example
A gNMI subscription sampling /interfaces/interface/state/statistics every 1 second with JSON_IETF or PROTO encoding to a collector.
Misconception
gNMI always requires Protocol Buffers. In practice gNMI can use JSON_IETF encoding for readability when interoperability or tooling requires it.
Key Takeaway

Select protocol and encoding based on performance needs and collector compatibility; both use YANG to define what is streamed.

screens.title: GPB, JSON, and XML for Telemetry
screens.narratorSegment: Telemetry data can be encoded in several formats; the chapter emphasizes Protocol Buffers, JSON, and XML. Google Protocol Buffers are a compact, binary serialization that requires a. proto definition; GPB typically yields smaller messages and faster parsing, which is beneficial at high ingest rates. JSON is text-based and human-readable, making debugging and lightweight tooling easier but producing larger payloads. XML is also human readable but usually more verbose. A concrete example: streaming the same interface-statistics message encoded with GPB will reduce network bytes and parsing time compared to JSON, which may simplify tool integration at the cost of bandwidth. A common misconception is that readability equals suitability; large-scale, high-frequency telemetry favors GPB for performance, while JSON can be used for lower-volume or when human inspection is necessary. The practical choice depends on collector parsing capabilities, storage costs, and network capacity. Takeaway: match encoding to scale and operational needs—use GPB when performance matters, JSON or XML when readability and ease of use are preferable. Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › GPB vs JSON vs XML
Data Formats

Protocol Buffers, JSON, XML

GPB
Binary, compact, requires .proto schema.
JSON
Human readable, larger payloads, broad tooling support.
XML
Readable but verbose; common with NETCONF.
Concrete example
Compare bytes on the wire for a one-second stream of interface stats encoded as GPB vs JSON to choose the right encoding for high-volume streams.
Misconception
Choosing JSON solely for readability without accounting for high ingest rates can lead to increased storage and parsing load.
Key Takeaway

Pick GPB for high-frequency, high-volume telemetry; use JSON or XML when human-readability or compatibility outweighs performance.

screens.title: End-to-End Telemetry Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable streaming telemetry architecture contains a sequence of components, each serving a focused role. First, network devices are telemetry publishers configured with sensor-groups that reference YANG paths and sampling intervals. Second, the telemetry collector receives and parses the streams; it can be an agent like Telegraf or a custom application that understands gNMI or NETCONF subscriptions. Third, for high-scale deployments, add a message broker to buffer and distribute streams, decoupling collectors from consumers and improving resilience. Fourth, store data in a time-series database optimized for high write rates, efficient time-based queries, and retention policies. Finally, visualize with tools such as Grafana. A concrete example maps: IOS XE device streams interface statistics → Telegraf gNMI input binds to a port → InfluxDB stores metrics → Grafana dashboards visualize trends. A common mistake is neglecting retention and aggregation: without summarization you will hit storage limits. Takeaway: design each component for scale and reliability and provide TLS and authentication across the chain to secure telemetry. End-to-End Telemetry Architecture means design for scale: publishers, collectors, optional brokers, tsdb storage, and dashboards—each tuned for throughput, durability, and security.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Telemetry Architecture
Architecture

End-to-End Telemetry Pipeline

Network Devices
Publish YANG-path data per sensor groups and subscriptions.
Telemetry Collector
Receives and parses gNMI/NETCONF streams; forwards to storage or broker.
Message Broker (optional)
Buffers and distributes streams for scale and decoupling.
Time-Series DB
Optimized for high ingest, retention, and time-based queries.
Processors / Consumers
Anomaly detectors, analytics, and enrichment pipelines.
Visualization
Grafana dashboards and alerts surface trends and thresholds.
Concrete example
IOS XE device streams interface statistics to Telegraf (gNMI input), Telegraf writes to InfluxDB, Grafana visualizes in-octets and out-octets.
Operational caution
Plan retention policies and aggregation to avoid unbounded growth in storage when sampling at high frequency.
Key Takeaway

Build pipelines that balance fidelity and cost: where needed, add brokers and aggregation to maintain performance and reliability.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › gNMI Subscribe (Python)
Code Walkthrough

Conceptual gNMI subscription

This conceptual snippet illustrates the connect, subscribe, and receive loop you'll implement with production client libraries.
# Conceptual gNMI subscribe (simplified and conceptual)
from gnmi import gnmi_pb2, gnmi_pb2_grpc
import grpc
import time

TARGET_IP = "192.168.1.101"
TARGET_PORT = 50051
USERNAME = "admin"
PASSWORD = "cisco"
INTERFACE_STATS_PATH = "/interfaces/interface[name='GigabitEthernet1']/state/statistics"

def subscribe_to_telemetry():
  channel = grpc.secure_channel(f"{TARGET_IP}:{TARGET_PORT}", grpc.ssl_channel_credentials())
  stub = gnmi_pb2_grpc.gNMIStub(channel)

  subscribe_request = gnmi_pb2.SubscribeRequest()
  subscribe_request.subscribe.mode = gnmi_pb2.SubscriptionList.STREAM
  subscribe_request.subscribe.encoding = gnmi_pb2.Encoding.JSON_IETF
  subscribe_request.subscribe.subscription.add(
    path=gnmi_pb2.Path(elem=[gnmi_pb2.PathElem(name=e) for e in INTERFACE_STATS_PATH.strip('/').split('/')]),
    mode=gnmi_pb2.SubscriptionMode.SAMPLE,
    sample_interval=1000000000
  )

  metadata = [('username', USERNAME), ('password', PASSWORD)]

  for response in stub.Subscribe(subscribe_request, metadata=metadata):
    if response.update:
      # Parse response.update.update[0].val.json_ietf_val or proto_bytes
      pass
    time.sleep(0.1)
Example detail
The sample interval in this snippet is 1 second (expressed in nanoseconds) to capture high-frequency interface metrics.
Caution
This code omits TLS cert handling, reconnection and robust parsing—add those in production clients.
Key Takeaway

The subscribe flow is connect, build subscription list, receive updates, parse encoding, and persist. Harden each step before production use.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety
screens.narratorSegment: Operational success depends on avoiding common pitfalls. Over-subscribing devices—requesting too many YANG paths or sampling too frequently—can overwhelm device C P U and collectors. Start with critical metrics and increase cadence only when needed. Security is mandatory: encrypt telemetry channels with TLS for gRPC or HTTPS for RESTCONF and authenticate collectors; if streams are unauthenticated they expose sensitive operational state. Data volume management is also essential: implement retention policies, aggregation, and downsampling so storage doesn't grow unbounded. Be careful with YANG path mismatches; the path in your subscription must match the device's YANG model and software version. Collector reliability matters: plan for high availability, retries, and broker-based buffering to prevent data loss. A concrete corrective step is to run a pilot with reduced point density and measure device load and network usage before scaling. Takeaway: balance fidelity against device and storage capacity, and secure every hop of the telemetry pipeline. Operational Considerations

Pitfalls and how to avoid them

  • Over-subscribing: Requesting too many metrics or too high a cadence can overload devices and collectors.
  • Security: Always use TLS and authenticate collectors to prevent unauthorized access to telemetry streams.
  • Data volume: Plan retention, aggregation, and summarization to limit storage growth.
  • YANG path mismatch: Verify paths against device software version and supported models.
  • Collector reliability: Ensure high availability and consider brokers for buffering.
Concrete mitigation
Pilot with a narrow set of YANG paths at moderate cadence, measure device and network load, then iterate toward production settings.
Common mistake to avoid
Assuming telemetry does not need the same operational security posture as other management interfaces—secure it the same way you secure config channels.
Key Takeaway

Design telemetry with controls for cadence, security, storage, and collector availability to avoid common operational failures.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll move from the familiar world of periodic polling to a push-based telemetry model that streams device data in near real time. You will learn why SNMP polling—where a management station asks devices for snapshots every few minutes—can miss transient events, and how streaming telemetry captures high-granularity operational state to enable faster troubleshooting and proactive detection. We will explore the main protocols that make streaming possible, including gNMI and NETCONF subscriptions, and the data formats those protocols commonly use: efficient binary encoding with Google Protocol Buffers and human-readable formats like JSON or XML. You’ll also see a practical, end-to-end architecture: devices push to a collector, messages can be buffered with a broker when needed, data lands in a time-series store, and dashboards visualize trends. By the end you’ll understand where streaming telemetry fits in an enterprise design and a simple scenario—collecting interface octets at sub-second intervals—to illustrate why this model matters operationally. Think about a recent transient outage: could higher-frequency telemetry have revealed a microburst earlier?

These objectives map what you will be able to do after completing the chapter. First, you will differentiate traditional SNMP polling from streaming telemetry by explaining the pull versus push pattern and the operational limits of polling when you need sub-second visibility. Second, you will explain the benefits and use cases of streaming telemetry—real-time visibility, higher granularity, and improved troubleshooting—so you can justify its adoption in an operational design. Third, you will describe common protocols such as gNMI and NETCONF subscriptions, and how they use YANG models with data encodings like Protocol Buffers or JSON to transmit structured data. Fourth, you will outline a basic collector architecture from devices to dashboards, and identify where message brokers and time-series databases fit. Each objective includes a short practical reason: these are the skills technicians and architects use to capture transient events, scale telemetry ingest, and build dashboards that surface meaningful alerts before users notice issues.

This second objectives slide explains practical demonstrations you can use to show competency. For differentiating polling and streaming, set up a short experiment: compare SNMP polled interface counters at five-minute intervals with a one-second telemetry subscription and note dropped transient events. For explaining benefits and use cases, produce a short report that uses streamed metrics to correlate C P U spikes with interface microbursts; this proves higher granularity helps root cause analysis. For describing gNMI and NETCONF subscriptions, map a YANG path to a device sensor and explain how protocol encoding—Protocol Buffers or JSON—affects payload size and parsing. Finally, for outlining architecture, draw a concise topology showing where a message broker may be required and justify the time-series database choice for retention and query patterns. Each demonstration builds confidence that you can design, configure, and reason about telemetry behavior in production networks.

Begin with a clear definition: SNMP polling is a pull-based model where a management station requests specific MIB objects periodically, producing discrete snapshots of device state. In contrast, streaming telemetry is a push-based model where devices continuously send operational data to a collector, often at sub-second rates. A concrete example helps: if you poll interface counters every five minutes, a brief microburst that causes packet loss for twenty seconds can be invisible in the five-minute snapshot. Streaming telemetry configured to sample every second will capture that microburst as a series of high-resolution points you can analyze. A common misconception is that polling is always lighter on the network; in large-scale deployments polling thousands of devices frequently creates larger aggregate overhead and C P U load than efficiently encoded, device-driven streams. To test this, compare aggregate bytes on the management plane during a polling schedule versus the same metrics streamed at one-second intervals encoded with Protocol Buffers. Takeaway: streaming gives fidelity and timeliness; however, you must design retention and volume controls so you don't overwhelm storage or processors. SNMP Polling vs Streaming Telemetry means polling gives periodic snapshots that can miss short events; streaming telemetry provides continuous, high-resolution data for accurate, proactive operations.. In practical terms, why polling snapshots miss transient events and how streaming fixes that. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Streaming telemetry is a push-based network monitoring model where devices send operational data to a collector without waiting for a poll. Define the model clearly: devices publish telemetry for configured YANG paths, and subscriptions control what is sent and at what cadence. Benefits are concrete: near real-time visibility lets you detect performance bottlenecks as they happen, higher granularity captures short-lived events, and scalability improves because devices decide what to send and when. A practical example: configure a sensor that streams interface in-octets every second for a critical uplink. The collector aggregates these samples and detects spikes that match a service degradation window. A common misconception is that streaming always increases network load; in practice, efficient encodings like Protocol Buffers reduce payload size and allow you to select only necessary YANG paths, minimizing overhead. Closing thought: streaming telemetry is a design pattern—use it where fidelity, timeliness, and proactive analytics matter most. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

gNMI and NETCONF subscriptions are the primary protocols for streaming telemetry covered in this chapter. Define gNMI as a gRPC-based interface that uses YANG to define data and typically encodes payloads with Google Protocol Buffers for efficient binary serialization. gNMI supports one-time retrievals and continuous subscriptions; subscription modes include sample and on-change, allowing you to tailor cadence and triggers. NETCONF subscriptions extend NETCONF to push updates, often using XML or JSON encodings and the same YANG models. A concrete example: a gNMI subscription might sample an interface statistics path every second with JSON IETF or PROTO encoding. A common misconception is that gNMI always uses GPB—some implementations allow JSON IETF encoding for readability. Why it matters: protocol and encoding choices affect payload size, parsing load, and interoperability with collectors and analytics engines. Takeaway: choose gNMI for high-performance streaming, and use NETCONF subscriptions when integrating into existing NETCONF-based management stacks. gNMI and NETCONF Subscriptions means gnmi is grpc-based and efficient with gpb; netconf subscriptions extend xml/json-based netconf to support pushes. both rely on yang for data modeling.. In practical terms, protocol roles, yang models, and subscription modes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Google Protocol Buffers are a compact, binary serialization that requires a. proto definition; GPB typically yields smaller messages and faster parsing, which is beneficial at high ingest rates. The practical choice depends on collector parsing capabilities, storage costs, and network capacity. Takeaway: match encoding to scale and operational needs—use GPB when performance matters, JSON or XML when readability and ease of use are preferable. A reliable streaming telemetry architecture contains a sequence of components, each serving a focused role. First, network devices are telemetry publishers configured with sensor-groups that reference YANG paths and sampling intervals. Second, the telemetry collector receives and parses the streams; it can be an agent like Telegraf or a custom application that understands gNMI or NETCONF subscriptions. Third, for high-scale deployments, add a message broker to buffer and distribute streams, decoupling collectors from consumers and improving resilience. Fourth, store data in a time-series database optimized for high write rates, efficient time-based queries, and retention policies. Finally, visualize with tools such as Grafana. Operational success depends on avoiding common pitfalls. Over-subscribing devices—requesting too many YANG paths or sampling too frequently—can overwhelm device C P U and collectors. Start with critical metrics and increase cadence only when needed. Security is mandatory: encrypt telemetry channels with TLS for gRPC or HTTPS for RESTCONF and authenticate collectors; if streams are unauthenticated they expose sensitive operational state. Data volume management is also essential: implement retention policies, aggregation, and downsampling so storage doesn't grow unbounded. Be careful with YANG path mismatches; the path in your subscription must match the device's YANG model and software version. Collector reliability matters: plan for high availability, retries, and broker-based buffering to prevent data loss. A concrete corrective step is to run a pilot with reduced point density and measure device load and network usage before scaling. Takeaway: balance fidelity against device and storage capacity, and secure every hop of the telemetry pipeline. Let's summarize the key concepts you should remember. First, streaming telemetry is a push-based model where devices continuously stream selected YANG-path data to a collector, providing near real-time visibility. Second, SNMP polling is pull-based and can miss transient events; it still has value for lower-frequency inventory or configuration checks but is limited for high-fidelity monitoring. Third, gNMI and NETCONF subscriptions are the principal protocols: gNMI is gRPC-based and often uses Protocol Buffers for efficiency, while NETCONF subscriptions extend XML/JSON-based NETCONF systems. Each concept supports design decisions for performance, scalability, and operational readiness. Keep these core ideas in mind as you design telemetry pipelines and choose protocols, encodings, and storage strategies.
